findings.title: Duplicate `downsize` definition silently replaces the (from, to, max_width, max_height) signature
findings.body: The file now defines `self.downsize` twice: once at line 145 taking `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` and again at line 149 taking `(from, to, dimensions, opts)`. In Ruby the second definition wins, so the 4-positional-argument version no longer exists. Any existing caller that passes width and height (e.g. `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, w, h)`) will now raise `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments`, and there is no indication all callers were migrated. One of the two definitions must be removed/renamed.

findings.title: Animated GIF downsize passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH
findings.body: The uploads controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)`. For animated GIFs, `optimize` selects `downsize_instructions_animated`, which delegates to `resize_instructions_animated` and produces `gifsicle ... --resize-fit 80% ...`. gifsicle does not accept a percentage for `--resize-fit`; the command fails, `convert_with` returns false, and the retry loop in the controller burns all 5 attempts without shrinking the file. Animated GIFs over the size limit can therefore never be uploaded, and the failure is silent (`&> /dev/null`).

findings.title: Downsize retry loop ignores failure and retries identical work
findings.body: The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > limit` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize` but never checks its boolean return value. If the conversion fails (bad image, missing convert/gifsicle, unsupported format), the file size never changes and the same failing command is executed 5 times synchronously inside the deferred job before falling through to `Upload.create_for`, which will then fail validation anyway. The result is wasted CPU and a confusing generic error instead of surfacing that the image could not be processed. Break out of the loop when `downsize` returns false.

findings.title: Client-side upload size limit hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring site settings
findings.body: `validateUploadedFile` previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so images and attachments each respected their configured limits. The change replaces that with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. Sites with `max_attachment_size_kb` above 10MB will now have the client reject attachments the server would accept, and sites with image limits above 10MB get a client-side rejection even though the server can now auto-downsize large images (which is the point of this PR — the client should not pre-emptively block oversized images anymore). The same hardcoding was applied to the 413 handler at line 246.

findings.title: Download cap hardcoded to 10MB for API URL uploads
findings.body: `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes`. While the intent is to allow downloading larger originals for downsizing, this also caps downloads for sites whose configured image limit is above 10MB (they could previously pull larger files), and it downloads full-size originals for non-image types too, with the size magic number duplicated between the controller and the JS client. This should derive from a single setting (e.g. a multiple of max_image_size_kb) rather than a literal.

findings.title: Downsizing SVGs and other vector/odd formats with `convert -resize 80%` can corrupt or balloon them
findings.body: The guard uses `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)`, which (matching the client-side list) includes SVG. Running ImageMagick `-resize 80%` on an SVG rasterizes it and writes the result over the original path with the `.svg` extension, producing a mislabeled raster file or a failure; repeated attempts can also grow the file, making the loop spin. SVGs (and potentially other formats that don't shrink meaningfully at 80% quality-agnostic resize) should be excluded from the auto-downsize path.

findings.title: Dead first `downsize` overload: width/height form unreachable and resize/downsize now inconsistent
findings.body: Beyond the duplicate-definition problem, the first `downsize` (line 145) builds `"#{max_width}x#{max_height}"` and forwards — but it is immediately overridden by the line-149 version that takes a raw `dimensions` string. Meanwhile `resize` still takes explicit width/height. The net effect is an API where `downsize(from, to, 100, 200)` compiles fine at call sites in other code but now treats `100` as the dimensions string and `200` as `opts`, silently producing `-resize 100` with a nonsense opts hash. Any caller using the old arity misbehaves rather than raising.
